general.source_sheet: General Advisory (fallback -- no specific domain category matched this question)

ordered_steps.title: Identify or restate the problem/context the question is actually about
guidance: A complete answer should make clear what specific issue, crop, or situation the recommendation addresses before giving the recommendation itself.

ordered_steps.title: Give the core recommendation that actually answers what was asked
guidance: This is the substantive advice: what to do, use, or decide.

ordered_steps.title: Specify quantity, dose, or rate, only if the question or recommendation genuinely involves one
guidance: Applicable only when a measurable quantity is relevant (e.g. chemical dose, seed rate, water volume) -- do not require this for questions that never involve a quantity.

ordered_steps.title: Specify timing or growth stage, only if relevant to the recommendation
guidance: Applicable only when timing or growth stage affects whether the recommendation is followed correctly.

ordered_steps.title: Note precautions, safety, or follow-up considerations where applicable
guidance: e.g. re-application intervals, safety precautions, or when to seek further expert help.

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct urgency
ordered_steps.example: Weeds at 3 weeks after sowing fall inside soybean's critical weed-competition window (roughly 30-45 days after sowing) - act now rather than delay, using hand/mechanical weeding or a timed post-emergence herbicide.
guidance: Flag the time-criticality immediately since that changes the urgency of the answer compared to a general weed question.

ordered_steps.title: Why this timing matters
ordered_steps.example: Weeds uncontrolled during the critical period cause yield loss that isn't fully recovered even if the weeds are removed later.

ordered_steps.title: Identify the dominant weed type first
ordered_steps.example: Check whether grassy weeds, broadleaf weeds, or sedges (e.g. Cyperus) dominate - herbicide choice, if used, depends on this.
guidance: This is the decision-branch step: herbicide recommendation cannot be given usefully without knowing weed type.

ordered_steps.title: Mechanical/manual control
ordered_steps.example: Hand weeding or inter-row hoeing at this stage is effective and avoids herbicide risk, though labour-intensive; often combined with one herbicide pass for larger areas.

ordered_steps.title: Chemical control
ordered_steps.example: An early post-emergence herbicide matched to the dominant weed type, applied at the recommended dose/water volume/growth-stage window from the current registered label for soybean.
guidance: Never name a fixed product/dose without matching it to the weed type identified in step 3.

ordered_steps.title: Preventing recurrence next season
ordered_steps.example: Stale seed-bed technique, clean bunds/channels, and crop rotation reduce the weed seed bank over successive seasons.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Act within the critical period using weed-type-matched mechanical or chemical control at the correct dose and timing; manage the seed bank going forward to reduce recurrence.

conditional_branches.condition_step: If the question is a specific compound question (e.g. product/dose/rotational or safety concerns), not a general how-do-I question

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct answer
ordered_steps.example: Herbicide choice depends on the dominant weed type and timing window (pre- vs. post-emergence); some soybean herbicides also carry soil-residual risk to a following wheat crop if dose or timing to wheat sowing isn't respected.
guidance: Answer all parts of the compound question together since they are linked by the same label check.

ordered_steps.title: Herbicide choice by timing window and weed type
ordered_steps.example: Pre-emergence (0-3 days after sowing, before weeds emerge - the more reliable option where grass-weed pressure is heavy, forms a soil-surface barrier) versus post-emergence (broadleaf-targeted, grassy-targeted, or broader-spectrum, used once weeds are already up); since this field is 3+ weeks past sowing, post-emergence is the relevant option now, but pre-emergence is worth planning for the next sowing.
guidance: Always present pre-emergence as the first-line option in principle, even when the farmer's specific timing has already passed it by - this is what lets the answer also serve the next season's planning, not just this one.

ordered_steps.title: Herbicide mode-of-action rotation
ordered_steps.example: Rotate between different herbicide modes of action across seasons rather than repeating the same product, since repeated use of the same mode of action speeds up resistance build-up in the weed population.

ordered_steps.title: PHI for this soybean crop (distinct from the wheat-carryover concern)
ordered_steps.example: Check the product's own pre-harvest interval (PHI) - the minimum wait before harvesting THIS soybean crop, so any residue decays to a safe level before the grain is eaten or sold.
guidance: This is a genuinely separate figure from the wheat-rotation interval in step 5 - do not conflate the two even though both appear on the same product label.

ordered_steps.title: Carryover risk to wheat - what decides it (a rotational-crop restriction, not PHI)
ordered_steps.example: Certain herbicide groups, particularly the imidazolinone group (e.g. imazethapyr-type actives), have documented soil-residual activity that can injure wheat if dose was exceeded, a longer-persistence product was used, or the gap to wheat sowing was too short; breakdown is slower in dry weather and in alkaline/high-pH soil.
guidance: This is the specific compliance point this narrow question is really asking about - treat it as central content, and name it correctly as a rotational crop restriction/plant-back interval rather than calling it PHI, since PHI and this are different concepts on the same label.

ordered_steps.title: How to check for this specific product
ordered_steps.example: Read the product's current label for any stated rotational-crop restriction or minimum waiting period before sowing wheat; this varies by active ingredient, and caution should increase (wait longer than the label's baseline) after an unusually dry spell.
guidance: Never state "it is safe" or "it is not safe" generically - route to the specific product's label every time.

ordered_steps.title: Reducing the risk
ordered_steps.example: Never exceed labelled dose, prefer a product without a flagged wheat-rotation restriction if wheat follows, and respect the minimum interval to next-crop sowing.

ordered_steps.title: Safety precautions while spraying
ordered_steps.example: Protective clothing, gloves and a mask while spraying, since skin contact with or inhalation of the herbicide can cause poisoning; avoid drift onto neighbouring susceptible crops; wash hands, face and equipment thoroughly afterward.
guidance: This was previously the one entry in the sheet with no PPE/spray-safety guidance despite being a herbicide-application answer - always include this step for any spray recommendation.

ordered_steps.title: Alternative sustainable methods - non-chemical control
ordered_steps.example: Hand-weeding or inter-row mechanical cultivation controls weeds effectively without any herbicide-residue carryover risk to a following sensitive crop like wheat.
guidance: This is the mandatory Alternative Sustainable Methods slot, and it doubles as a way to sidestep the carryover risk this question is centrally about.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Match herbicide timing/type to the weed situation at label dose, separately confirm this product's own PHI (for this soybean harvest) and its distinct wheat-rotation restriction (for next season) on the same label, follow spray safety precautions and mode-of-action rotation, and consider hand-weeding as a carryover-free alternative.

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct schedule
ordered_steps.example: Irrigate Bt cotton under drip every 2-3 days through the flowering-to-boll stage rather than on a fixed weekly schedule.
guidance: Give the frequency answer immediately since that is the literal question asked.

ordered_steps.title: Why this stage is critical
ordered_steps.example: Flowering through boll development is cotton's most water-sensitive window; both moisture stress and waterlogging at this stage cause flower/boll shedding and directly cut final yield.

ordered_steps.title: Drip-specific scheduling logic
ordered_steps.example: Drip should run more frequently in smaller amounts than flood irrigation, to hold a steady root-zone moisture level rather than a wet-dry cycle; adjust frequency for soil type (sandy = more frequent/shorter, heavy = longer intervals).

ordered_steps.title: Monitoring instead of a fixed calendar
ordered_steps.example: Checking soil moisture at root depth where feasible is more reliable than a rigid schedule, since local weather and canopy stage shift actual demand day to day.

ordered_steps.title: Alternative sustainable methods
ordered_steps.example: Inter-row mulching conserves soil moisture and reduces irrigation frequency; skip irrigation immediately after a good rainfall event.
guidance: This is the mandatory Alternative Sustainable Methods slot before the conclusion.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: 2-3 day drip cycles through flowering-boll stage, adjusted for soil and weather, protect yield at cotton's most decisive growth window.

conditional_branches.condition_step: If the question is a specific compound question (e.g. product/dose/rotational or safety concerns), not a general how-do-I question

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct cause
ordered_steps.example: Emitters not releasing water evenly is almost always clogging - physical (sediment), mineral (hard-water deposit) or biological (algae/slime) - and the cleaning method depends on which type is present.

ordered_steps.title: Diagnostic check
ordered_steps.example: Inspect the residue type on affected emitters (crusty=mineral, slimy=biological, sandy/debris=physical) and note whether the problem is field-wide (filter issue) or localised (specific lateral/pipe damage).
guidance: This diagnostic step must come before any chemical treatment, since the wrong treatment (e.g. acid on a biological clog) wastes effort.

ordered_steps.title: Flushing procedure
ordered_steps.example: Open end caps on main, sub-main and then lateral lines and run water until it clears; clean or backwash the filter unit, since a clogged filter is a common field-wide cause.

ordered_steps.title: Targeted chemical treatment by clog type
ordered_steps.example: Mild acid flush (manufacturer-recommended dilution) for mineral deposits; low-concentration chlorine flush for biological/algae growth; manually clean or replace emitters still blocked afterward.
guidance: Never mix acid and chlorine treatments in the same flush cycle - flag this explicitly as a safety/compatibility caution.

ordered_steps.title: Alternative sustainable/preventive methods
ordered_steps.example: Upgrade to finer disc/screen filtration and adopt routine scheduled flushing rather than reactive cleaning only after emitters fail.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Identify the clog type first, flush lines and filter, apply the matched acid/chlorine treatment only where needed, and maintain filtration/flushing as ongoing prevention.

cultural.source_sheet: Domain-wise Answer Structures - Cultural and Crop Management Practices

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct figures
ordered_steps.example: About 60 cm row spacing, 20-25 cm plant-to-plant spacing, and 4-5 cm sowing depth are the general starting figures for a good maize stand.
guidance: Give the numeric answer immediately since that's the literal ask, before explaining the reasoning.

ordered_steps.title: Why spacing matters
ordered_steps.example: Spacing sets plant population, which decides how much light/water/nutrient each plant gets; too dense weakens plants and cob filling, too sparse wastes yield potential.

ordered_steps.title: Why sowing depth matters
ordered_steps.example: Too shallow exposes seed to moisture stress and bird/rodent loss; too deep delays or reduces emergence.

ordered_steps.title: Recommended practice with adjustment factors
ordered_steps.example: 60 cm x 20-25 cm as the default, tightened for hybrids specifically bred for high density or widened under rainfed/lower fertility; 4-5 cm depth, deeper only if surface soil is dry.
guidance: This is the compression point where a narrower question (e.g. "gap-filling" question below) pulls just the establishment-check step.

ordered_steps.title: Supporting practices for a uniform stand
ordered_steps.example: Good-quality treated seed at the recommended seed rate, fine well-prepared seedbed with adequate (not excess) moisture, and early post-emergence inspection for gaps.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: 60 cm x 20-25 cm spacing at 4-5 cm depth is the default; fine-tune for the specific hybrid's recommended density and field moisture at sowing.

conditional_branches.condition_step: If the question is a specific compound question rather than a general how-do-I question

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct fix
ordered_steps.example: Gap-fill promptly with pre-germinated seed of the same variety; patchy germination is usually caused by uneven sowing depth, poor seed quality, soil crusting, or moisture/pest problems at sowing.

ordered_steps.title: Diagnose the likely cause
ordered_steps.example: Uneven depth, poor germination %, soil crusting after rain, waterlogged/dry patches, or pest damage to germinating seed - check which applies before deciding if gap-filling alone is enough.

ordered_steps.title: Gap-filling method
ordered_steps.example: Pre-soak fresh seed of the same variety to pre-germinate it, then sow into the gaps as soon as possible (ideally within 1-2 weeks of original sowing) so the new seedlings can compete with the established crop.
guidance: Timing is the critical variable here - flag that late gap-filling produces plants that add little to final yield.

ordered_steps.title: Preventing recurrence next time
ordered_steps.example: Use a seed drill or careful manual spacing for uniform depth, use seed with confirmed high germination %, and avoid sowing right before/during heavy expected rainfall.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Act quickly with pre-germinated same-variety seed to fill gaps while the main crop is still young, and address whichever underlying cause (depth, seed, crusting, moisture, pest) applies for next season.

organic.source_sheet: Domain-wise Answer Structures - Organic and Natural Farming

ordered_steps.title: Introduction - clarify which system is actually meant
ordered_steps.example: "Organic" and "natural inputs" point to two distinct, differently-regulated Indian systems (Organic Farming under NPOP/PGS-India vs. Natural Farming/BPKP under the National Mission on Natural Farming); clarify which one fits the farmer's actual goal before recommending inputs.
guidance: Do not silently treat "organic" and "natural farming" as interchangeable - conflating them is a common and consequential mistake, since the permitted-input rules and the supporting government scheme differ between the two.

ordered_steps.title: The actual distinction
ordered_steps.example: Organic Farming: certification-driven (NPOP/PGS-India), permits external inputs like FYM/compost/vermicompost/certified biofertilisers, aimed at premium/certified markets. Natural Farming (BPKP/ZBNF): zero external input of any kind (chemical or organic), on-farm-only inputs from desi cow resources and local biomass, aimed at near-zero input cost.
guidance: This is the core fact the whole answer hinges on; state it plainly rather than letting the farmer infer it.

ordered_steps.title: Decision point - which path fits the farmer's goal
ordered_steps.example: Premium/certified market access -> Organic Farming path; lowest possible input cost and self-reliance -> Natural Farming path.
guidance: Let the farmer's own goal (stated or implied) decide the branch, rather than defaulting to one path.

ordered_steps.title: Organic Farming path - soil-building and certification
ordered_steps.example: FYM/compost/vermicompost/green manure (e.g. dhaincha) during land preparation; PGS-India group certification (more accessible for 2 acres than individual NPOP certification); certified external biofertilisers/biopesticides permitted.

ordered_steps.title: Natural Farming path - on-farm-only inputs
ordered_steps.example: Jeevamrit (soil microbial activity) and beejamrit (seed treatment) made from desi cow dung/urine, jaggery, pulse flour and local soil; mulching and whapasa (correct soil moisture management) as core practices; no external input of any kind, connects to the state's BPKP/Natural Farming mission rather than organic certification.

ordered_steps.title: Managing pests, disease and weeds (common to both paths)
ordered_steps.example: Crop rotation, resistant variety choice, field sanitation, biological control agents, and mechanical/cultural weeding replace synthetic pesticide/herbicide use under either system.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Choose Organic Farming (external permitted inputs + PGS-India certification) for certified/premium market access, or Natural Farming/BPKP (on-farm-only inputs, no external input at all) for near-zero cost; pest/disease/weed management is shared across both, and both need a multi-season transition.

conditional_branches.condition_step: If the question is a specific compound question rather than a general how-do-I question

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct method
ordered_steps.example: Jeevamrit is a fermented cow-dung, cow-urine, jaggery and pulse-flour preparation, fermented 5-7 days and then applied to soil or as a foliar spray to support soil biology.

ordered_steps.title: Ingredients and mixing
ordered_steps.example: ~10 kg fresh cow dung, 5-10 litres aged cow urine, ~2 kg jaggery (or ripe banana), ~2 kg pulse flour, a handful of undisturbed field soil, in ~200 litres of water.

ordered_steps.title: Fermentation process
ordered_steps.example: Stir thoroughly twice daily, ferment in the shade for 5-7 days; ready when it develops a pleasant fermented smell and visible microbial activity.

ordered_steps.title: Application method and frequency
ordered_steps.example: Apply via irrigation water or as a soil drench around the root zone, or diluted as a foliar spray, at roughly 15-20 day intervals through the season; one ~200-litre batch typically covers about one acre per application.

ordered_steps.title: Related preparation - the genuine alternative (Ghana Jeevamrit, not beejamrit)
ordered_steps.example: Ghana Jeevamrit (solid/dried jeevamrit): ~100 kg desi cow dung + ~1 kg jaggery + ~1 kg pulse flour + a handful of field soil, moistened with desi cow urine into balls/cake, shade-fermented 48 hours, then sun-dried, broken up and sieved into a powder that stores up to a year and is broadcast onto soil - this is the actual field/soil-application alternative to liquid jeevamrit; beejamrit is a different, seed-treatment-only preparation and is not a substitute here.
guidance: Correcting this matters because beejamrit and jeevamrit serve different purposes (seed treatment vs. ongoing soil application) - a farmer asking specifically about jeevamrit needs a jeevamrit-family alternative, not an unrelated seed-treatment product.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Prepare and ferment the liquid mixture for 5-7 days and apply roughly every 15-20 days through the season, or prepare Ghana Jeevamrit (solid form) when a storable, transportable version is more practical.

climate.source_sheet: Domain-wise Answer Structures - Climate, Weather & Stress Management

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / immediate priorities
ordered_steps.example: Right after hail damage this close to harvest: assess salvageable yield, watch for secondary fungal infection at wound sites, and report the loss for insurance promptly.
guidance: Post-event recovery questions need an action-priority list up front, not a general explanation of hail damage.

ordered_steps.title: Assess the extent of damage
ordered_steps.example: Distinguish structurally intact plants (partial harvest can still recover yield) from badly lodged/shattered areas (may need early harvest).

ordered_steps.title: Watch for secondary fungal infection
ordered_steps.example: Hail wounds are entry points for fungal disease, especially in humid post-storm weather; inspect over following days and be ready with a protectant fungicide if lesions appear.

ordered_steps.title: Harvest timing decision
ordered_steps.example: Harvest badly damaged areas early to recover remaining grain rather than risk further loss; continue normal timing for less-affected areas.

ordered_steps.title: Insurance and documentation
ordered_steps.example: Report the loss to the insurer/bank within the scheme's stipulated time window (e.g. under PMFBY) since delayed reporting can affect claim eligibility; photograph the damage as evidence.
guidance: Route insurance procedure specifics to the Credit/Loan & Insurance domain if the farmer's question shifts fully to the claim process itself.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Triage the field by damage severity, guard against wound-site disease, adjust harvest timing accordingly, and file an insurance report promptly if covered.

conditional_branches.condition_step: If the question is a specific compound question rather than a general how-do-I question

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct guidance
ordered_steps.example: Hold off irrigating now if soil moisture isn't critically low and substantial rain is genuinely expected within two days; irrigating right before rain risks waterlogging and wasted water.

ordered_steps.title: Wheat's critical-stage irrigation calendar
ordered_steps.example: CRI (~20-25 DAS, most critical of all), Tillering (~40-45 DAS), Late Jointing (~60-65 DAS), Flowering/heading (~80-90 DAS, second most critical), Milk stage (~100-105 DAS), Dough stage (~115-120 DAS, least critical/skippable); under limited water, prioritise CRI, flowering, then tillering/jointing, treating milk/dough as skippable first.
guidance: This is the concrete schedule that lets the farmer self-locate on the calendar and judge urgency, rather than only being told "it depends on growth stage" in the abstract - always give the actual day-ranges and priority order, not just the stage names.

ordered_steps.title: When to hold off
ordered_steps.example: Crop not at a critical stage (or at a low-priority one like late jointing/dough), and forecast rain expected to be substantial - skip irrigation to avoid the double-watering waterlogging effect.

ordered_steps.title: When to irrigate anyway
ordered_steps.example: Crop currently at or near CRI or flowering (wheat's two most critical stages) with visible moisture stress, or forecast is light/uncertain for the specific location - irrigate now rather than risk the critical stage.
guidance: This decision fork is the actual content of the question - always present both branches, not just one default answer.

ordered_steps.title: Using a reliable, local forecast source
ordered_steps.example: Check IMD forecast and local agromet advisory for the specific district rather than a general regional forecast, since local rainfall can vary significantly.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Base the decision on which stage of the irrigation calendar the crop is actually at, plus the forecast's specificity/reliability for the exact location, not the forecast headline alone; confirm the exact locally recommended schedule via KVK/state package of practices.

mechanisation.source_sheet: Domain-wise Answer Structures - Farm Tools & Mechanisation

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct guidance
ordered_steps.example: For a straightforward 2-acre job, a power tiller is generally the more cost-effective choice; a tractor-rotavator combination becomes worthwhile for speed, heavier soil, a tillage-intensive crop, or larger-scale needs.

ordered_steps.title: Deciding factor - soil type and tillage depth
ordered_steps.example: Power tiller suits lighter/medium soils and shallower tillage typical of small-holding preparation; tractor-rotavator handles heavier soil and deeper tillage more efficiently.

ordered_steps.title: Deciding factor - which crop is going into the field
ordered_steps.example: Paddy needs multiple puddling passes under standing water (to seal the soil and control weeds), which favours a tractor-rotavator even at 2 acres; vegetables and other fine-seedbed crops need shallower, finer tilth, which a power tiller handles well without paying for unneeded tractor-scale capacity.
guidance: This factor is as decisive as soil type but easy to overlook when the question is framed purely as tiller-vs-tractor economics - always ask what crop is going in before answering.

ordered_steps.title: Deciding factor - turnaround time
ordered_steps.example: At 2 acres, power tiller timing is usually adequate unless working under a tight window between two crops, where the tractor-rotavator's greater speed can justify its higher cost.

ordered_steps.title: Deciding factor - cost comparison
ordered_steps.example: Compare local per-acre/per-hour hiring rates at the Custom Hiring Centre (CHC) or Farm Machinery Bank, including fuel and operator cost, since rates vary by location.

ordered_steps.title: Practical decision rule
ordered_steps.example: Light-to-medium soil, vegetable/fine-seedbed crop, no time pressure -> power tiller; heavier soil, a tillage-intensive crop like paddy, urgent turnaround, or combinable with other tractor operations -> tractor-rotavator.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Default to the power tiller for a routine 2-acre job on light-medium soil going into a vegetable or similar crop; switch to tractor-rotavator when speed, soil type, a tillage-intensive crop like paddy, or combined operations change the economics.

conditional_branches.condition_step: If the question is a specific compound question rather than a general how-do-I question

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct answer
ordered_steps.example: Apply through the state's farm mechanisation subsidy scheme (e.g. under SMAM), via the state portal, local CSC, or Block Agriculture Office, using Aadhaar, land record and bank details; approval typically must come before purchase.

ordered_steps.title: Eligibility and category-based subsidy
ordered_steps.example: Open to individual farmers, with small/marginal, women, or SC/ST categories often eligible for a higher subsidy percentage than the general category.

ordered_steps.title: Documents required
ordered_steps.example: Aadhaar card, land ownership/tenancy record, bank account for DBT of the subsidy amount.

ordered_steps.title: How and where to apply
ordered_steps.example: State agricultural mechanisation/DBT Agriculture portal, in person at Block/District Agriculture Office, or via a Common Service Centre (CSC); exact portal/process varies by state.
guidance: Never give one fixed portal name/URL as universal - route to the state's current scheme page since this varies by state and changes over time.

ordered_steps.title: Approval and purchase sequencing
ordered_steps.example: Wait for application approval and confirmed subsidy percentage/empanelled dealer list before purchasing, since a pre-approval purchase may not be honoured for subsidy.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Apply via the state portal/CSC/Block office with the standard documents, and purchase only after approval to ensure the subsidy is honoured.

postharvest.source_sheet: Domain-wise Answer Structures - Post-Harvest Management & Storage

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct answer
ordered_steps.example: Good onion storage starts at harvest, not just at the storage structure; onion monsoon rot is mainly a moisture/ventilation problem, fixed with correct harvest timing, proper curing, a raised well-ventilated storage structure, and regular inspection.

ordered_steps.title: Harvest at the correct maturity stage
ordered_steps.example: Harvest at neck fall (roughly 50-70% of plants' tops naturally falling over and starting to dry/yellow); too-early harvest (upright green tops) gives high-moisture, poorly-sealed-neck bulbs prone to rot, too-late harvest risks splitting/sunburn/re-sprouting - both shorten storage life regardless of how good the storage structure is afterward.
guidance: This is the step most farmers skip when they think of "storage" as starting only after the crop leaves the field - good storage outcomes are decided partly at harvest.

ordered_steps.title: Curing before storage
ordered_steps.example: Field-cure for about 1-2 weeks in shade with full neck drying before storing; inadequately cured bulbs carry excess moisture that promotes rot.

ordered_steps.title: Storage structure
ordered_steps.example: Ventilated shed/mesh-wall structure or slatted racks rather than closed rooms or plastic sacks; store in thin layers, not thick heaps, since heaps trap heat and moisture centrally.

ordered_steps.title: Keeping storage elevated and dry
ordered_steps.example: Raised off the ground, away from direct rain and dampness, since monsoon humidity is the main driver of onion storage rot.

ordered_steps.title: Ongoing monitoring
ordered_steps.example: Inspect every 1-2 weeks during monsoon and remove rotting/sprouting/softening bulbs immediately to stop spread to neighbouring bulbs.

ordered_steps.title: Alternative/traditional low-cost method
ordered_steps.example: Traditional raised bamboo/mesh-slat ventilated onion storage structures used in onion-growing regions are purpose-built for this exact monsoon problem.
guidance: This is the Alternative Sustainable Methods slot - a low-cost, non-mechanical option before the conclusion.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Correct harvest-stage timing, full curing, thin-layer storage in a raised ventilated structure, and regular inspection together control monsoon rot in stored onions.

conditional_branches.condition_step: If the question is a specific compound question rather than a general how-do-I question

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct answer
ordered_steps.example: Small beetles in stored wheat are typically Rice Weevil or a similar storage pest; the current infestation needs a direct answer, but almost all real control of this problem is preventive/structural, not a reach-for-chemical response - the same preventive steps also stop recurrence.
guidance: Lead with the fact that prevention, not cure, is the primary defence, even while answering the farmer's immediate "how do I get rid of them" question directly.

ordered_steps.title: Confirming the cause
ordered_steps.example: Storage insects multiply fastest above ~10-12% grain moisture or in a previously infested, dirty storage structure with entry gaps - check all three before deciding on treatment.

ordered_steps.title: Prevention - treat the structure, seal entry points, ensure ventilation
ordered_steps.example: Clean and, where there is a pest history, treat the empty storage room/bin (floor, walls, cracks) before every storage cycle; seal cracks and rodent holes that let pests (and rodents) in; ensure proper ventilation to avoid damp pockets that favour both mould and insects; use any grain-protectant treatment prophylactically (on clean grain at bagging, or on the empty structure) rather than only after an infestation is visible.
guidance: This is the step the farmer's question doesn't explicitly ask for but most needs to see - present it as the foundation, not an afterthought, since a farmer who only treats this one infestation without fixing the structure will see it recur.

ordered_steps.title: Non-chemical corrective steps for the current infestation
ordered_steps.example: Sun-dry grain to below the safe moisture level (weevils/borers can't multiply below ~10% moisture); empty and clean the storage structure, sweeping out dust/residue that harbours insects; apply the structural treatment/crack-sealing from step 3 before restocking.

ordered_steps.title: Chemical treatment (only if needed)
ordered_steps.example: A registered grain-protectant treatment or fumigation (by trained, licensed personnel for fumigants, since an improperly used fumigant releases a toxic gas that can cause poisoning if inhaled) only if infestation persists after drying/cleaning, strictly per label dose and required aeration period before use.
guidance: Never apply insecticide directly onto grain meant for near-term consumption without confirming it's approved for stored-grain use at that dose - this is a food-safety-adjacent caution worth its own line.

ordered_steps.title: Alternative sustainable methods
ordered_steps.example: Clean dry neem leaves/neem oil mixed into grain, or hermetically sealed storage that suffocates insects by oxygen depletion - effective chemical-free options for smaller household quantities.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Handle the current batch by correcting moisture and cleaning the structure first, reserving chemical treatment/fumigation for persistent infestation only; for every cycle after this, structural prevention (clean, sealed, ventilated storage, used prophylactically) is the primary defence, not chemical control.

market.source_sheet: Domain-wise Answer Structures - Market Prices, MSP & Marketing

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct process
ordered_steps.example: Register as a farmer-seller with the state's procurement system, bring quality-compliant paddy to your nearest notified procurement centre, and get paid via direct bank transfer for MSP sale.

ordered_steps.title: Registration requirement
ordered_steps.example: Advance registration (online portal or at the centre) with Aadhaar, land records/crop-area declaration, and bank account details is typically required before selling.

ordered_steps.title: Where to sell
ordered_steps.example: Sell at the notified procurement centre nearest you (state civil supplies corporation, cooperative federation, or FCI depending on the state); confirm the current season's active centre list for your district.
guidance: Never assume the same centre/agency applies across all states - this varies by state's procurement arrangement.

ordered_steps.title: Quality norms and process at the centre
ordered_steps.example: Produce must meet Fair Average Quality (FAQ) norms for moisture and foreign matter; dry grain properly before bringing it to avoid rejection or a discounted rate.

ordered_steps.title: Payment process
ordered_steps.example: Weighing and quality check at the centre, with payment credited directly to the registered bank account within the scheme's stated timeline.

ordered_steps.title: Alternative channels if MSP procurement isn't convenient
ordered_steps.example: Local APMC mandi at prevailing price, e-NAM if the mandi is linked, or an FPO for collective marketing and potentially better price realisation.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Register ahead, meet quality norms, sell at the nearest active procurement centre for MSP, or use mandi/e-NAM/FPO channels as alternatives.

conditional_branches.condition_step: If the question is a specific compound question rather than a general how-do-I question

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct answer
ordered_steps.example: Check the Agmarknet portal or the e-NAM portal/app for your district and commodity for today's mandi-wise price; call the mandi office directly as a backup if internet access is limited.

ordered_steps.title: Using Agmarknet
ordered_steps.example: Publishes daily modal/min/max prices by state, district and commodity across notified mandis, useful for comparing prices across nearby mandis before transporting produce.

ordered_steps.title: Using e-NAM
ordered_steps.example: If the local mandi is e-NAM-linked, the portal/app shows live bidding prices and arrivals, and may allow online bidding for better price transparency and reach.

ordered_steps.title: Other accessible sources
ordered_steps.example: Kisan Suvidha app, local KVK or Block Agriculture Office, or a direct call to the mandi office are simple backups if internet access is inconvenient.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Use Agmarknet/e-NAM as the primary current-price check, cross-check with a direct mandi call, and compare across nearby mandis before deciding to sell.

schemes.source_sheet: Domain-wise Answer Structures - Agricultural Schemes & Subsidies

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct list
ordered_steps.example: Core relevant schemes for a small 1.5-acre farmer: PM-KISAN (income support), Kisan Credit Card (credit), PMFBY (insurance), plus PMKSY/SMAM/Soil Health Card for input support.
guidance: Name the actual schemes immediately rather than saying "several schemes are available" without naming them, per the no-vague-recommendation rule.

ordered_steps.title: What is actually being grown also decides the scheme list
ordered_steps.example: 1.5 acres confirms small/marginal-farmer status, but whether the land is under agricultural (cereals/pulses/oilseeds/cotton, Dept. of Agriculture) or horticultural (fruits/vegetables/spices/flowers/plantation, Dept. of Horticulture, MIDH) classification determines a partly different scheme catalogue, department, and often a different subsidy percentage for a similar input.
guidance: This is easy to miss since "1.5 acres" sounds like it fully defines the farmer's situation, but commodity/land classification is an independent, equally decisive variable - ask or confirm it rather than assuming field-crop schemes are the complete list.

ordered_steps.title: Direct income and credit support
ordered_steps.example: PM-KISAN direct annual income support via DBT; Kisan Credit Card for subsidised-interest crop credit, extendable to allied activities.

ordered_steps.title: Input and infrastructure support
ordered_steps.example: PMKSY/Per Drop More Crop for micro-irrigation, SMAM for machinery subsidy suited to a small holding, Soil Health Card for soil-test-based nutrient recommendations.

ordered_steps.title: Insurance
ordered_steps.example: PMFBY crop insurance at a low farmer premium share, particularly valuable for a small holding's risk exposure.

ordered_steps.title: Category-based and state-specific add-ons
ordered_steps.example: Woman/SC-ST/other category farmers may get a higher subsidy percentage on some schemes; states often run additional top-up schemes - confirm which schemes are actually active in the farmer's specific state before applying.
guidance: Never claim state-specific scheme details without prompting confirmation of the actual state and whether that scheme runs there, per the state-specific-scheme rule.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion and standing scheme-question note
ordered_steps.example: PM-KISAN, KCC and PMFBY as core support, layered with PMKSY/SMAM/Soil Health Card for inputs and cross-checked against agricultural-vs-horticultural classification; scheme rules change over time and by state, so confirm current, local details with the Block Agriculture Office or Horticulture Office rather than treating this list as final.
guidance: Apply this closing pattern (confirm state availability + route to the local Block Agriculture/Horticulture office for the latest update) to every government-scheme-related answer, not only this one.

conditional_branches.condition_step: If the question is a specific compound question rather than a general how-do-I question

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct answer
ordered_steps.example: Apply through the state's PMKSY micro-irrigation subsidy portal or Block/District Horticulture Office, with approval and empanelled-vendor selection required before installation.

ordered_steps.title: Eligibility and documents
ordered_steps.example: Open to individual farmers, often a higher subsidy percentage for small/marginal farmers; Aadhaar, land record, bank account for DBT.

ordered_steps.title: Application process and vendor requirement
ordered_steps.example: Apply via state portal or Block/District Horticulture Office; select from the empanelled/approved drip-vendor list, since subsidy is usually tied to an approved supplier.
guidance: This empanelled-vendor requirement is the detail most likely to trip up a farmer who installs first through a local, non-approved installer - flag it clearly.

ordered_steps.title: Sequencing - approval before installation
ordered_steps.example: Apply and receive approval before installing; installing ahead of approval or via a non-empanelled vendor risks losing subsidy eligibility.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion and standing scheme-question note
ordered_steps.example: Apply through the state portal/office with standard documents, choose an empanelled vendor, and install only after approval; confirm the scheme is currently active in the farmer's specific state, and check with the local Block Agriculture/Horticulture Office for the latest position.
guidance: Apply this same closing pattern (confirm state-specific availability + route to local office for the latest update) to every government-scheme-related answer.

credit.source_sheet: Domain-wise Answer Structures - Credit, Loan & Insurance

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct process and rate
ordered_steps.example: Apply at a bank branch (commercial/cooperative/RRB) or online; base interest rate is typically ~7% per annum on the eligible limit, reduced further with prompt repayment under interest subvention.
guidance: Name the actual current rate range directly rather than saying "a subsidised rate applies" without a figure, then flag that it should be confirmed with the bank since rates are periodically revised.

ordered_steps.title: Eligibility
ordered_steps.example: Owner-cultivators, tenant farmers, oral lessees/sharecroppers in many states, and farmers in animal husbandry/fisheries under the KCC extension to those sectors.

ordered_steps.title: Documents required
ordered_steps.example: Identity/address proof (Aadhaar), land ownership/tenancy record, passport-size photographs.

ordered_steps.title: How to apply
ordered_steps.example: Apply at the nearest bank branch or online via the bank's KCC portal; PM-KISAN beneficiaries can use a simplified linked application process in many cases.

ordered_steps.title: How the credit limit and interest rate are set
ordered_steps.example: Credit limit based on landholding, cropping pattern and scale of finance; base rate ~7% p.a. up to the scheme limit (commonly ₹3 lakh), with subvention reducing the effective rate further for prompt repayment.

ordered_steps.title: Renewal requirement
ordered_steps.example: KCC needs periodic review/renewal with the issuing bank to keep the limit active and retain the subvented rate.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion and standing scheme-question note
ordered_steps.example: Apply at a bank branch or online with standard documents; expect ~7% base rate reduced by subvention for prompt repayment, confirmed exactly by the bank since rate/subvention terms are revised periodically.

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct process
ordered_steps.example: Confirm your cotton crop/area is notified and enrolled under PMFBY; a widespread drought loss is typically assessed via area-level yield data (Crop Cutting Experiments) rather than an individual claim form, with payout at the block/area level.

ordered_steps.title: Confirming coverage first
ordered_steps.example: Check notification status of your crop/village for this season and your enrollment status (often automatic if loanee, separate application if non-loanee) before assuming a claim can proceed.
guidance: This is the essential gating step - a farmer cannot claim for a crop/area that isn't notified/enrolled, so it must come before any process explanation.

ordered_steps.title: How a drought-type (area) loss is actually assessed
ordered_steps.example: Area-based yield assessment through Crop Cutting Experiments (CCEs) at the notified area level, comparing actual average yield against the threshold yield for that crop/area - different from an individual per-farmer damage report.
guidance: This distinction (area-yield-based vs individual-loss-based) is the core misconception to correct for this specific question.

ordered_steps.title: Reporting an individual/localised event alongside
ordered_steps.example: If there's also specific localised damage to report individually, intimate via the insurer's helpline/app, your bank, or local agriculture/insurance office within the scheme's stated time window (commonly 72 hours for such events); the official Krishi Rakshak Helpline (toll-free 14447) can guide on the correct next step.
guidance: Give the actual, current official helpline number directly rather than a vague "contact the insurer" - a farmer in an active drought/loss situation needs an actionable number now.

ordered_steps.title: Payment process
ordered_steps.example: Payout is disbursed to the bank account once area-level yield shortfall is confirmed, generally without individual field inspection for an area-yield-based scheme.

ordered_steps.title: If delayed or rejected
ordered_steps.example: Escalate through the bank/insurer's grievance mechanism, the Krishi Rakshak Helpline (14447), or the local Agriculture Department/District Collector's office.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion and standing scheme-question note
ordered_steps.example: Confirm notification/enrollment, understand the area-yield-based assessment mechanism for a drought loss, use 14447 or the grievance channel if payment is delayed or disputed; PMFBY's notified-crop list and terms are reviewed each season, so confirm the current, area-specific position with the local Block Agriculture Office.
guidance: Apply this same closing pattern (confirm state/season-specific availability + route to local Block Agriculture Office for the latest update) to every government-scheme-related answer.

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct contacts
ordered_steps.example: Contact the Kisan Call Centre (1800-180-1551), your Block/District Agriculture Officer, or your nearest KVK; KVK is the strongest option for in-person diagnosis of a genuinely unfamiliar pest.
guidance: Name the actual toll-free number directly, per the rule against vague "contact your local officer" answers without specifics.

ordered_steps.title: Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK)
ordered_steps.example: District KVK plant-protection specialists can identify the pest via field visit/sample inspection and give tailored management guidance - the strongest option for a genuinely novel problem.

ordered_steps.title: Block/District Agriculture or Horticulture Officer
ordered_steps.example: Locally accessible extension staff who can help with identification and immediate guidance, and connect to relevant schemes if the issue is area-wide.

ordered_steps.title: Kisan Call Centre
ordered_steps.example: Toll-free 1800-180-1551, staffed by subject-matter experts, useful as a quick first opinion before deciding if an in-person visit is needed.

ordered_steps.title: Other advisory channels
ordered_steps.example: Kisan Suvidha app and state SMS agro-advisories for a quick photo-based query or general advisory, though in-person expert confirmation is best for a genuinely novel pest.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Start with a phone-based first opinion (Kisan Call Centre or Block office), then follow up with an in-person KVK visit if the pest remains unclear, since correct identification must come before any control recommendation.

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct answer
ordered_steps.example: Contact your district KVK directly by phone or in person to check their current training calendar and register for their next organic farming batch - registration is arranged locally by the KVK, not through a central portal.

ordered_steps.title: Finding the schedule
ordered_steps.example: Each KVK maintains its own season/year training calendar including organic/natural farming; schedules vary by KVK and update periodically, so a direct enquiry is the reliable method.

ordered_steps.title: Registration process
ordered_steps.example: Register directly with the KVK (often free or nominal fee), providing basic details; seats per batch are typically limited.

ordered_steps.title: What the training typically includes
ordered_steps.example: Classroom sessions, on-farm demonstrations (composting, vermicomposting, natural input preparation), sometimes an exposure visit to an organic demonstration farm.

ordered_steps.title: Related opportunity
ordered_steps.example: Some KVKs can connect interested participants to PGS-India group certification if formal organic certification is a later goal.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: A direct call or visit to the district KVK is the reliable way to find and register for the next organic farming training batch.

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct process
ordered_steps.example: Apply at the local DISCOM sub-division office or the state electricity board's online portal with land/identity documents and load (pump HP) details; feasibility check and load sanction follow before installation.

ordered_steps.title: Application requirements
ordered_steps.example: Land ownership/tenancy documents, identity proof, tubewell pump load (HP) details; many states have a distinct agricultural-connection category and tariff.

ordered_steps.title: Feasibility and load sanction
ordered_steps.example: The department checks nearest transformer/feeder capacity; inadequate infrastructure may need an upgrade, with cost-sharing arrangements varying by state policy.

ordered_steps.title: Costs, timeline, and asking about a connection subsidy
ordered_steps.example: Security deposit, service line/meter charges, possible infrastructure augmentation charges; DISCOM communicates a target timeline after feasibility confirmation. Actively ask the DISCOM whether the state currently offers a capital subsidy, subsidised augmentation charges, or a concessional agricultural tariff for the new connection itself, since several states have such support and it isn't always volunteered.
guidance: This is the specific gap worth flagging - farmers often only hear about PM-KUSUM (the solar alternative) and don't think to ask whether the grid-connection route itself is separately subsidised in their state.

ordered_steps.title: Alternative - solar pump under PM-KUSUM
ordered_steps.example: A PM-KUSUM solar pump avoids the grid-connection process entirely and carries a capital subsidy, worth considering if grid connection is slow or costly in the area.
guidance: This is the natural cross-reference to Farm Tools & Mechanisation/Schemes without duplicating that domain's full process here.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion and standing scheme-question note
ordered_steps.example: Apply through the DISCOM with standard documents and load details, expect a feasibility-based timeline, ask specifically about any state connection subsidy, and consider PM-KUSUM solar as an alternative; confirm both the connection-subsidy policy and PM-KUSUM terms with the local DISCOM/Block Agriculture Office since these vary by state and change periodically.
guidance: Apply this same closing pattern (confirm state-specific availability + route to local office for the latest update) to every government-scheme-or-subsidy-related answer.

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct answer
ordered_steps.example: Apply through your state's PM-KUSUM implementing agency (renewable energy agency or Agriculture Department) portal, with land/water-source details; subsidy is a central+state+farmer share, and installation must be via an empanelled vendor.

ordered_steps.title: Eligibility and documents
ordered_steps.example: Individual farmers with a reliable water source (borewell/well/canal/pond); Aadhaar, land record, bank account details.

ordered_steps.title: Application process
ordered_steps.example: Apply via the state's designated implementing agency portal, providing water-source details and required pump capacity based on irrigation area and crop water need.

ordered_steps.title: Subsidy structure and vendor requirement
ordered_steps.example: Central + state + farmer-share subsidy structure (farmer share sometimes loan-financed); installation only through an empanelled vendor from the state's approved list.

ordered_steps.title: Site verification before approval
ordered_steps.example: Site verification confirms water-source adequacy and installation suitability before final pump capacity and subsidy amount are confirmed; installation follows only after approval.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion and standing scheme-question note
ordered_steps.example: Apply through the state PM-KUSUM agency/portal, complete site verification, and install only via an empanelled vendor after approval; confirm the component is currently active in the farmer's specific state, and check with the local Block Agriculture Office for the latest position.
guidance: Apply this same closing pattern (confirm state-specific availability + route to local office for the latest update) to every government-scheme-related answer.

livestock.source_sheet: Domain-wise Answer Structures - Animal Husbandry & Livestock

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / triage framing
ordered_steps.example: A sudden milk-yield drop usually traces to feed/water change, heat stress, calving-cycle timing, or an early health/udder problem - the response depends on which of these applies, checked systematically.
guidance: Frame this as a triage checklist since the question is diagnostic, not a single fixed answer.

ordered_steps.title: Check feed and water first
ordered_steps.example: Recent change in feed quantity/quality or a gap in feeding schedule is the most common cause; inadequate water intake also directly cuts yield.

ordered_steps.title: Check for udder or general health warning signs
ordered_steps.example: Udder swelling, heat, pain, or abnormal milk (clots, blood, foul smell) points to mastitis/infection; fever, reduced appetite or dullness alongside the yield drop are general-health warning signs.
guidance: This is the decision-branch step - presence of any of these signs should redirect the farmer to veterinary care rather than feed troubleshooting.

ordered_steps.title: Check calving-cycle timing
ordered_steps.example: Yield naturally changes around the dry period and around recent calving - rule this out as a normal, non-problem explanation before assuming something is wrong.

ordered_steps.title: If management-related - corrective action
ordered_steps.example: Correct the feed ration (adequate green/dry fodder, concentrate, mineral mixture), ensure free clean water access, and manage heat stress with shade and cooler-time feeding; recovery expected within a few days.

ordered_steps.title: If health-related - do not self-treat
ordered_steps.example: Any udder or general-illness warning sign should prompt a veterinary visit rather than a feed adjustment or home remedy.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Rule out the easy, common causes (feed, water, heat, cycle timing) first; treat any udder or illness warning sign as a veterinary priority rather than a management fix.

conditional_branches.condition_step: If the question is a specific compound question rather than a general how-do-I question

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct diagnosis
ordered_steps.example: Swollen, painful udder with clotted milk is mastitis, an udder infection requiring prompt veterinary treatment rather than home management alone.
guidance: Name the condition directly per the direct-answer rule, while being explicit that home treatment alone is not sufficient here - this is a case where the honest answer includes "see a vet," not a home fix.

ordered_steps.title: Confirm it is mastitis, not another problem
ordered_steps.example: Localised udder swelling/pain plus clotted milk from that specific quarter distinguishes mastitis from a systemic problem like milk fever (general weakness/staggering, no udder-specific signs); report any additional systemic symptoms to the vet too.
guidance: This identification/differential-check gate applies even though the symptoms already point strongly to mastitis - ruling out a systemic condition needing separate treatment is the equivalent of the crop-side "confirm identification before treating" gate.

ordered_steps.title: Why veterinary assessment is necessary
ordered_steps.example: Severity and infection type vary, and the correct antibiotic/route/duration needs direct veterinary assessment - guessing at home risks the infection becoming chronic or spreading to other quarters.

ordered_steps.title: What to do while arranging veterinary care
ordered_steps.example: Continue milking out the affected quarter completely and frequently (discard that milk); keep the animal in a clean, dry area; do not mix affected-quarter milk with milk for sale/use.

ordered_steps.title: Veterinary treatment
ordered_steps.example: Typically an intramammary antibiotic infusion (sometimes plus injectable antibiotic for severe cases) with anti-inflammatory support as needed; complete the full prescribed course.
guidance: Never suggest a specific antibiotic or dose in the main text - this is a veterinary-prescribed treatment, analogous to the "confirm with the current registered label" rule for crop chemicals.

ordered_steps.title: Milk-withholding period
ordered_steps.example: Observe the veterinarian-specified withholding period after the last treatment dose before using that milk for consumption or sale - the livestock equivalent of a crop PHI.
guidance: Always pair antibiotic treatment with this withholding-period caution, mirroring the mandatory PHI pairing rule used for crop chemicals throughout this project.

ordered_steps.title: Preventing recurrence
ordered_steps.example: Milking hygiene (clean hands/udder, teat dip if available), clean dry housing, and prompt attention to any future udder injury or early symptom.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Confirm it is mastitis and not a systemic issue, treat this as needing prompt veterinary care, maintain milking-out and hygiene in the meantime, complete the full prescribed course, and strictly observe the milk-withholding period.

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct starting guidance
ordered_steps.example: Prepare the pond (liming, manuring, adequate depth), stock a composite Catla-Rohu-Mrigal combination of Indian Major Carps at appropriate density, and maintain feeding/water-quality routines.

ordered_steps.title: Pond preparation
ordered_steps.example: Dry pond bed if possible, apply lime then manure about a week before stocking to build natural plankton food; ensure adequate water depth (1.5-2 m) and check for leakage/predator-fish entry.

ordered_steps.title: Species selection
ordered_steps.example: Catla (surface), Rohu (column), Mrigal (bottom) composite culture uses different pond zones/feeding niches without direct competition - the standard reliable starting combination for most freshwater ponds in India.

ordered_steps.title: Stocking density and sourcing
ordered_steps.example: A few thousand fingerlings per acre total across the combination for semi-intensive management, adjusted to feeding intensity; source healthy fingerlings from a reliable government/certified hatchery, not an unknown source.

ordered_steps.title: Feeding and water-quality management
ordered_steps.example: Supplementary feed (rice bran + oil cake mix, or commercial floating feed) alongside natural pond food from manuring; monitor for early-morning gasping at the surface as an oxygen-depletion warning sign.

ordered_steps.title: Alternative sustainable methods
ordered_steps.example: Paddy-cum-fish culture or small backyard biofloc systems as alternative or complementary low-cost, space-efficient options.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Proper pond preparation, a composite carp stocking combination from a reliable hatchery, and consistent feeding/water-quality monitoring are the foundation of a half-acre pond fish farming start.

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct diagnosis
ordered_steps.example: Early-morning gasping with mortality is dissolved oxygen depletion, most often from excess organic load (overfeeding, manuring, or an algae bloom) - act with emergency aeration immediately.
guidance: Name the actual mechanism (oxygen depletion) directly, since a farmer facing active fish mortality needs the diagnosis and the emergency action together, not separately.

ordered_steps.title: Why it happens at this specific time
ordered_steps.example: Oxygen is produced by plankton during the day but consumed by all pond life overnight; a heavy bloom or decomposing organic matter drives oxygen to its lowest point right before sunrise - exactly when gasping/mortality appears.

ordered_steps.title: Immediate emergency action
ordered_steps.example: Agitate the water surface for aeration, add fresh water if available to dilute organic load, and stop feeding immediately until stabilised.
guidance: This is time-critical - sequence it before the underlying-cause analysis, since delay costs fish.

ordered_steps.title: Identifying the underlying cause afterward
ordered_steps.example: Check whether recent feeding/manuring was excessive for the pond's size and biomass, and check water colour/clarity for an overly dense algae bloom needing partial water exchange.

ordered_steps.title: Preventing recurrence
ordered_steps.example: Feed only what fish consume in a reasonable time (not a fixed excess), monitor water colour/fish behaviour especially in warm weather, and consider an aerator for ponds with repeat history.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Treat this as oxygen depletion - act immediately with aeration and reduced feeding, then correct the feeding/manuring level and monitor going forward to prevent recurrence.

allied.source_sheet: Domain-wise Answer Structures - Allied Agricultural Activities

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct starting guidance
ordered_steps.example: Choose a suitable bee species (Apis cerana indica or Apis mellifera), start with a modest number of colonies and standard hive equipment, site the apiary well, and learn seasonal management - with crop pollination as a bonus benefit.

ordered_steps.title: Choosing the bee species
ordered_steps.example: Apis cerana indica is generally easier for beginners and suited to smaller diversified farms; Apis mellifera gives higher honey yield but needs more intensive management.

ordered_steps.title: Getting started - colonies, equipment, site
ordered_steps.example: Start with a handful of colonies from a reliable local beekeeper/KVK/cooperative, standard hive equipment (boxes, frames, smoker, veil, gloves), sited with shade, wind protection, and access to diverse forage.

ordered_steps.title: Basic seasonal management
ordered_steps.example: Colony strengthening before the main flow season, sugar-syrup feeding during forage-scarce dearth periods, and monitoring for wax moth, mites and absconding.

ordered_steps.title: Protecting bees during your own crop spraying
ordered_steps.example: Avoid insecticide application during active bee foraging hours or flowering periods, since your own crop-protection sprays can harm the very colonies you're keeping.
guidance: This cross-references back to the pest-management domain's pollinator-protection guidance without duplicating it.

ordered_steps.title: Honey harvesting and support available
ordered_steps.example: Harvest once combs are capped/mature; support and training available through the National Beekeeping and Honey Mission and local KVK.

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: A locally suited species, a modest starter setup from a reliable source, and learning the seasonal management calendar are the basics; honey income plus improved crop pollination are the combined return.

conditional_branches.condition_step: If the question is a specific compound question rather than a general how-do-I question

ordered_steps.title: Introduction / direct diagnosis
ordered_steps.example: Webbing and larvae damaging wax combs is wax moth infestation, one of the most common bee-enemy problems, arising mainly in weak or poorly managed colonies.

ordered_steps.title: Why it takes hold
ordered_steps.example: Wax moth larvae feed on wax/pollen/debris and succeed specifically in weak colonies or where empty comb space exceeds what the bee population can actively guard.

ordered_steps.title: Immediate cleanup
ordered_steps.example: Remove and destroy heavily webbed/damaged combs, scrape and clean the hive box of larvae/eggs/debris, and reduce hive space to match the current bee population.

ordered_steps.title: Strengthening the colony (the real long-term fix)
ordered_steps.example: Identify and address why the colony is weak (queen problem, disease, inadequate feeding), since cleanup alone without strengthening the colony typically leads to reinfestation.
guidance: This is the step that distinguishes a lasting fix from a temporary one - always include it, not just the cleanup steps.

ordered_steps.title: Protecting stored (non-hive) comb
ordered_steps.example: Store spare comb frames in a well-ventilated, light-exposed area (wax moth prefers dark, undisturbed conditions) and inspect periodically.

ordered_steps.title: Alternative sustainable methods
ordered_steps.example: Freezing stored comb briefly, or a bee-safe approved fumigation method specifically for stored comb (never for comb with an active colony present).

ordered_steps.title: Conclusion
ordered_steps.example: Clean out the current wax moth infestation, right-size hive space, and fix the underlying colony weakness, since a strong colony is the best lasting defence.
